name: Maiden Lane LLCs

summary.text: Maiden Lane LLC, Maiden Lane II LLC and Maiden Lane III LLC were three limited liability companies created by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York in 2008 with Federal Reserve Board authorization. Maiden Lane LLC (March 2008) borrowed about $28.82 billion from the New York Fed to hold roughly $30 billion of Bear Stearns assets in connection with JPMorgan Chase's acquisition of Bear Stearns. Maiden Lane II LLC (December 2008) borrowed $19.5 billion to buy residential mortgage-backed securities from the securities lending portfolios of AIG insurance subsidiaries. Maiden Lane III LLC (November 2008) borrowed about $24.3 billion, with a $5 billion AIG equity contribution, to buy multi-sector CDOs from AIG Financial Products' credit default swap counterparties, which then terminated the swaps. BlackRock managed the portfolios. All three loans were repaid with interest; the New York Fed reported net gains of about $2.5 billion (ML), $2.8 billion (ML II) and $6.6 billion (ML III).

facts.claim: On March 16, 2008 the Federal Reserve Board authorized the New York Fed to make a senior loan to Maiden Lane LLC to buy about $30 billion of less liquid Bear Stearns assets, to facilitate JPMorgan Chase's acquisition of Bear Stearns. At closing on June 26, 2008 the New York Fed lent $28.8 billion and JPMorgan Chase lent $1.1 billion, subordinated for repayment to the New York Fed's loan. The New York Fed gives the original loan amount as $28.82 billion.
facts.quote: On March 16, 2008, the Board authorized the New York Reserve Bank to make a senior loan to a limited liability company, Maiden Lane LLC ... at closing on June 26, 2008 ... the New York Reserve Bank actually lent $28.8 billion to Maiden Lane, and JPMorgan Chase actually lent $1.1 billion. / The original amounts of these loans were $28.82 billion and $24.3 billion respectively.

The New York Fed put the securities' face value at about $39.3 billion and their fair value at about $20.8 billion as of October 31, 2008.

facts.claim: Maiden Lane III LLC borrowed approximately $24.3 billion from the New York Fed (principal balance at closing $24,339 million), alongside a $5.0 billion equity contribution from AIG, to purchase multi-sector CDOs from AIG Financial Products' credit default swap counterparties. The New York Fed put the CDOs' estimated fair value at about $29.6 billion against a face value of about $62.1 billion as of October 31, 2008; the Federal Reserve Board described that valuation as substantially below par.

facts.claim: SIGTARP's November 17, 2009 audit found that after limited efforts to negotiate concessions from AIG's counterparties failed, the New York Fed decided to pay them at what was effectively face or 'par value': the counterparties kept about $35 billion in collateral already posted and terminated their CDS contracts with AIGFP, bringing the total to $62.1 billion, effectively the par value of the swaps. SIGTARP concluded that FRBNY's negotiating strategy offered little opportunity for success even though one counterparty (UBS) was willing to make a 2 percent concession if the others did. SIGTARP noted no TARP funds were directly used in the Maiden Lane III transaction. (SIGTARP audit finding.)
facts.quote: FRBNY's negotiating strategy to pursue concessions from counterparties offered little opportunity for success, even in light of the willingness of one counterparty to agree to concessions. / after limited efforts to negotiate concessions from the counterparties failed, FRBNY decided to pay AIG's counterparties at what was effectively face or 'par value'

facts.claim: According to SIGTARP, FRBNY contacted eight of AIG's largest counterparties by telephone over a two-day period to seek concessions; only UBS was willing to make a modest 2 percent concession if the others did so, and the rest refused. SIGTARP also reported that Mr. Geithner and Mr. Bernanke did not participate in the counterparty payment negotiations, and that Geithner and the FRBNY general counsel told SIGTARP that the counterparties' financial condition was not a relevant factor in the decision to create Maiden Lane III and pay counterparties effectively at par. A January 2010 House Oversight staff report said internal FRBNY communications contradicted that account.
facts.quote: FRBNY contacted by telephone eight of AIG's largest counterparties over a two-day period and attempted to obtain such concessions from the counterparties. / Mr. Geithner and Mr. Bernanke did not participate in the counterparty payment negotiations.

facts.claim: The Congressional Oversight Panel's June 10, 2010 report on the AIG rescue concluded that the government did not use its negotiating leverage with AIG's counterparties, that every counterparty received exactly the same deal, a complete rescue at taxpayer expense, and that the government averted a financial collapse but put billions of taxpayer dollars at risk, changed the marketplace and adversely affected public confidence in the market. The panel recorded that Secretary Geithner later testified he believed payment in full to all AIG counterparties was necessary to stop a panic. (Congressional Oversight Panel finding.)
facts.quote: every counterparty received exactly the same deal: a complete rescue at taxpayer expense / Secretary Geithner later testified that he believed that payment in full to all AIG counterparties was necessary to stop a panic

facts.claim: On March 15, 2009, after public and congressional pressure and after consultation with the Federal Reserve, AIG disclosed the identities of its counterparties. Reuters reported that Goldman Sachs and a group of European banks were the major beneficiaries of $93 billion in payments from AIG; Goldman received an aggregate $12.9 billion through three types of transactions (collateral for credit default swaps, purchases of CDOs, and payments to counterparties of a securities lending program); Société Générale received $11.9 billion, Deutsche Bank $11.8 billion and Barclays $8.5 billion.

facts.claim: In a January 2013 SEC filing, AIG's board stated that, in view of the positions of the counterparties, the time pressures posed by the November 10 deadline and the limited bargaining power that could be employed without regulatory abuse, the only workable course was to pay essentially par to the counterparties. The same filing quoted a GAO report stating that all counterparties were paid effectively par value for the credit default swaps.

facts.claim: Maiden Lane III LLC repaid the New York Fed's loan with interest on June 14, 2012; proceeds from further sales repaid AIG's equity contribution plus accrued interest by July 16, 2012; and on August 23, 2012 the New York Fed announced the sale of ML III's remaining securities, estimating a net gain of about $6.6 billion for the public, including $737 million in accrued interest on the loan. The New York Fed said the sales were conducted by BlackRock Solutions. New York Fed President William Dudley described the sale as closing an important chapter, the Fed's assistance to AIG.
facts.quote: Net proceeds from past sales, conducted by BlackRock Solutions, as well as cash flow the securities generated while held by ML III, enabled the full repayment of the loan and AIG's equity / closing an important chapter—our assistance to AIG—that was undertaken to stabilize the financial system in the midst of the financial crisis

facts.claim: On March 24, 2008 the New York Fed published a summary of terms for its financing of JPMorgan Chase's acquisition of Bear Stearns: a $29 billion loan backed by a $30 billion portfolio of Bear Stearns assets valued as of March 14, 2008, plus a $1 billion subordinated note from JPMorgan Chase absorbing the first losses. Both loans went to a Delaware limited liability company, each with a 10-year term renewable by the New York Fed; the Fed loan carried the primary credit rate (then 2.5 percent), the JPMorgan note that rate plus 450 basis points. BlackRock Financial Management was retained by the New York Fed to manage and liquidate the assets.

openQuestions: The brief's '$93.2 billion' total was not found verbatim in any source. The components reported from AIG's March 15, 2009 disclosure are now recorded: $22.4 billion CDS collateral and $12.1 billion municipal GIAs (AIG release), $27.1 billion Maiden Lane III payments and $43.7 billion securities lending (Risk.net, CNBC, House Oversight staff report). The three non-municipal components sum to $93.2 billion and all four to $105.3 billion, which would account for both the Reuters '$93 billion' and the Bloomberg-sourced '$105 billion' headlines; Bloomberg's own March 2009 report says 'about $100 billion'. The owner should confirm the sums against Attachments A-D of the release (the attachments were not retrieved) and note that the securities-lending window differs between sources (September 18 to December 12 per Risk.net; September 18 to December 31 per an AIG chart reproduced on Scribd).

The New York Fed's Maiden Lane page and its January 19, 2010 statement give ML III payments to counterparties as $26.8 billion (plus $2.5 billion to AIGFP); SIGTARP and COP summaries give a fair market value of about $27.1 billion, and Risk.net and the House Oversight staff report also use $27.1 billion. All are recorded as their sources state them; the owner may want to reconcile.
The New York Fed's own September 2018 press release on the final Maiden Lane LLC sale was not retrieved (only Bloomberg Law's report and third-party reprints); the Bloomberg Law report is cited.

The Maiden Lane II borrowing date (December 12, 2008) and the $22.5 billion authorization appeared in search results tied to the New York Fed's Maiden Lane II page and AIG subsidiary filings; the page attribution should be checked with check-links.mjs and a read of the page.
The exact Maiden Lane III closing date (November 2008) was not quoted by a retrieved page; the date field is left at month precision.
Geithner's start date as New York Fed president (November 2003) was not confirmed by a retrieved source; only the January 26, 2009 end of his tenure is sourced.
